schema_notes.first_mention_year: Integer year of earliest documented attestation (negative values = BCE; null if not extracted from retrieved summary and flagged for manual check).
schema_notes.is_historical_867: Boolean: true if the barony title name is historically authentic for the 867 AD start date; false if anachronistic or unattested <= 867 (candidate for Step 2 resolution).
schema_notes.named_after_post_867_person: Boolean: true if the title name incorporates a person/dynasty/settler after 867 AD.
schema_notes.natural_proper_name: Object indicating whether the title derives from a hydronym, oronym, choronym, or other natural topographic feature.
schema_notes.morphemes: List of constituent roots/morphemes with source language and English translation.
schema_notes.older_name_by_867: Object indicating whether a distinct older name STRICTLY ATTESTED <= 867 AD exists for the settlement (or its immediate predecessor site / base name without a post-867 modifier). Every exists=true entry carries first_mention_year <= 867.

b_halab.first_mention_attestation: Ebla and Mesopotamian cuneiform tablets (late 3rd millennium BCE) as Halab / Armi

morphemes.translation: white (or milking, per folk etymology; ancient Semitic toponym)

b_halab.etymology_analysis: Ancient Semitic toponym attested in 3rd-millennium BCE Eblaite and Mesopotamian cuneiform sources (Halab/Khalpe), preserved continuously into Arabic Halab; renamed Beroea in the Hellenistic period.

current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Anachronistic foundation evaluated in 1122 Imperial Chancellery audit.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Seleucus I Nicator (c. 300 BCE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Hellenistic and Roman-Byzantine official name alongside the indigenous Semitic name Halab.

b_tall_afrin.first_mention_attestation: 19th century CE (founded as a market town)

morphemes.language: Arabic / Kurdish (from Latin Ufrenus / Greek Oinoparas)

b_tall_afrin.etymology_analysis: Compound toponym meaning 'Mound of Afrin', named after the Afrin River (Assyrian Apre, Seleucid Oinoparas, Roman Ufrenus); the modern settlement of Afrin was founded as a market town only in the 19th century.

older_name_by_867.notes: The Afrin River was attested in antiquity (Apre, Oinoparas, Ufrenus), but the settlement of Afrin / Tall Afrin was founded in the 19th century.

b_azaz.first_mention_attestation: Hurrian (Azazuwa), Old Aramaic (Hzz), and Neo-Assyrian (Hazazu, 9th century BCE); Abbasid-era visit by Ishaq al-Mawsili (767-850 CE)

morphemes.language: Arabic (from Hurrian Azazuwa / Aramaic Hzz / Assyrian Hazazu)

b_azaz.etymology_analysis: Pre-classical toponym attested as Hurrian Azazuwa, Old Aramaic Hzz, and Neo-Assyrian Hazazu, continuing as Medieval Greek Azazion and Arabic A'zaz / Azaz (attested under Abbasid rule via Ishaq al-Mawsili, 767-850 CE).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Hurrian and Neo-Assyrian records
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Hurrian, Aramaic, Neo-Assyrian, and Byzantine forms of the same toponym.

b_manbij.first_mention_attestation: Pre-Alexandrine Aramaic coins (4th century BCE) reading Manbug (Mnbg)
b_manbij.etymology_analysis: Derived from Aramaic Manbug ('site of the spring'), attested on pre-Hellenistic coinage; rendered in Syriac as Mabbog, Greek as Bambyce and Hierapolis, and Arabic as Manbij.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Neo-Assyrian records (Nappigu) and Hellenistic Greek sources (Bambyce, Hierapolis)
older_name_by_867.notes: Assyrian and Greco-Roman names for the same city.

b_buzaa.first_mention_attestation: Crusader/medieval chronicles recording Roger of Antioch's capture of Buza'a in 1119 CE
b_buzaa.etymology_analysis: Medieval Arabic toponym (Buza'a / Bizaah) attested from the 12th century (1119 CE), evolving from the Roman-era settlement name Beselatha.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Roman imperial sources / Digital Atlas of the Roman Empire
older_name_by_867.notes: Known as Beselatha during the Roman Empire before becoming Buza'a in the Middle Ages.

b_qinnasrin.first_mention_attestation: Early Islamic conquest of Syria (637 CE, capital of Jund Qinnasrin) from Syriac Qennesrin
b_qinnasrin.etymology_analysis: From Syriac Qennesrin ('Nest of Eagles'), Arabicized as Qinnasrin upon the Muslim conquest in 637 CE; previously known in Hellenistic and Roman times as Chalcis ad Belum.

current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Resolved via verified historical center Chalkîs-in-Sîrjen documented in tarraconian_titles_1059.md.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Appian (founded by Seleucus I Nicator, r. 305-281 BCE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Hellenistic and Roman name (Chalcis ad Belum) predating the Syriac/Arabic name Qinnasrin.

b_artah.first_mention_attestation: Byzantine reconquest of Artah in 966 CE under Nikephoros II Phokas
b_artah.etymology_analysis: Medieval town and fortress east of the Iron Bridge on the Antioch-Aleppo road, first prominently attested in 966 CE during the Byzantine reconquest of northern Syria.

b_ar-rikha.first_mention_attestation: Roman/Eastern Roman era (peaked 240-350 CE; captured by Rashidun army in 636 CE)
b_ar-rikha.etymology_analysis: Ancient Northwest Syrian town (Ariha / Riha, rendered Ar-Rikha), attested in Roman/Byzantine times (240-350 CE) and captured by the Rashidun Caliphate in 636 CE as part of Jund Qinnasrin.

b_suriya.first_mention_attestation: Roman imperial sources (1st century CE Sura, Notitia Dignitatum, Procopius)
b_suriya.etymology_analysis: Arabicized form (Suriya) of the ancient Roman/Byzantine Euphrates fortress city of Sura, attested since the 1st-3rd centuries CE on the Strata Diocletiana.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Roman imperial sources and Notitia Dignitatum
older_name_by_867.notes: Classical Latin/Greek form of the same site name.

b_khunasira.first_mention_attestation: Pliny the Elder (c. 77 CE) as Chenneseri; early Islamic Khunasira (residence of Caliph Umar II, r. 717-720 CE)
b_khunasira.etymology_analysis: Attested by Pliny the Elder as Chenneseri and in early Islamic sources as Khunasira (residence and burial place of Umayyad Caliph Umar II, r. 717-720); known as Anasartha in the Byzantine era.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Pliny the Elder (Chenneseri) and Byzantine ecclesiastical records (Anasartha, 426 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Classical Roman (Chenneseri) and Byzantine (Anasartha) names for the same town.

b_ar-rusafa.first_mention_attestation: Neo-Assyrian cuneiform sources (9th century BCE) as Rasappa / Rasaappa

morphemes.translation: paved way / ancient Assyrian camp name

b_ar-rusafa.etymology_analysis: Continuously attested from 9th-century BCE Neo-Assyrian Rasappa (Biblical Rezeph, Ptolemy Rhesapha, Roman Rosafa) into Arabic al-Rusafa; renamed Sergiopolis in the Byzantine era.

current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Anachronistic foundation evaluated in 1122 Imperial Chancellery audit.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Neo-Assyrian cuneiform records and Byzantine sources (Procopius)
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Assyrian/Biblical forms and Byzantine Christian names (Sergiopolis, Anastasiopolis) of the same site.

b_siffin.first_mention_attestation: Battle of Siffin (657 CE / 37 AH) in early Islamic historiography

morphemes.translation: Byzantine-era village name on the Euphrates

b_siffin.etymology_analysis: Ruined Byzantine-era village on the right bank of the Euphrates near Raqqa, famously attested in 657 CE as the site of the Battle of Siffin during the First Fitna.

b_alexandretta.first_mention_attestation: Medieval Western pilgrim and Crusader sources (12th century diminutive Romance form Alexandretta)
b_alexandretta.etymology_analysis: Diminutive Romance form ('little Alexandria') coined by medieval Western pilgrims in the Crusader era, derived from the ancient Hellenistic foundation Alexandria ad Issum (333 BCE).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Hellenistic foundation commemorating the Battle of Issus (333 BCE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Founded as Alexandria (Alexandria ad Issum) in the Hellenistic period before the medieval diminutive Alexandretta appeared.

b_qurus.first_mention_attestation: Founded shortly after 300 BCE by Seleucus I Nicator as Cyrrhus (Arabicized Qurus / Qorosh after 637 CE)
b_qurus.etymology_analysis: Arabicized form (Qurus / Qorosh, attested from the 637 CE Arab conquest) of Greek Kyrrhos (Latin Cyrrhus), founded shortly after 300 BCE by Seleucus I Nicator and named after Cyrrhus in Macedonia.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Seleucus I Nicator (c. 300 BCE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Hellenistic/Roman name Cyrrhus and Byzantine ecclesiastical name Hagioupolis.

b_baghras.first_mention_attestation: Strabo's Geographica and Pliny the Elder as Pagrae; early Islamic events recorded by al-Baladhuri (c. 638 CE)

morphemes.translation: fortress name in the Amanus Mountains

b_baghras.etymology_analysis: Arabicized form (Baghras) of the ancient fortress name Pagrae, attested by Strabo and Pliny the Elder guarding the Syrian Gates in the Amanus Mountains.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Strabo's Geographica and Pliny the Elder
older_name_by_867.notes: Classical Greco-Roman form of the fortress name.

b_antiocheia.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 300 BCE by Seleucus I Nicator
b_antiocheia.etymology_analysis: Founded in 300 BCE by Seleucus I Nicator and named Antiocheia after his father Antiochus; capital of the Seleucid Empire and later Roman Syria.

b_as-suwaydiya.first_mention_attestation: Al-Muqaddasi (985 CE) listing Suwaydiyya among the principal towns of Jund Qinnasrin

morphemes.translation: the black one (diminutive, in reference to local roe deer)

b_as-suwaydiya.etymology_analysis: Arabic name al-Suwaydiyya ('the black one', referring to local roe deer), first attested in the late 10th century (al-Muqaddasi, 985 CE) as the medieval port of Antioch, succeeding Byzantine Port Saint Symeon and ancient Seleucia Pieria.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Seleucid foundation Seleucia Pieria (300 BCE) and 6th-century Byzantine port St. Symeon
older_name_by_867.notes: Seleucia Pieria (founded 300 BCE) was ruined by the 526 CE earthquake and succeeded by the 6th-century port of St. Symeon.

b_latakia.first_mention_attestation: Founded in the late 4th century BCE by Seleucus I Nicator as Laodikeia

morphemes.translation: city of Laodice (mother of Seleucus I)

b_latakia.etymology_analysis: Founded in the 4th century BCE as Laodikeia on the Coast by Seleucus I Nicator in honor of his mother Laodice; preserved in Arabic as al-Ladhiqiyya and Europeanized as Latakia.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Seleucus I Nicator (late 4th century BCE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Original Hellenistic Greek and Latin forms of the name.

b_jabala.etymology_analysis: Bronze Age coastal city attested in Ugaritic archives c. 1200 BCE as Gb'ly (Gibala), later Classical Gabala and Arabic Jabala / Jableh.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Ugaritic archives (c. 1200 BCE) and Greco-Roman sources (Gabala)
older_name_by_867.notes: Bronze Age and Greco-Roman forms of the same toponym.

b_baalbak.first_mention_attestation: Pre-Hellenistic Phoenician Ba'albek (b'lbk), renamed Heliopolis by Alexander the Great in 334 BCE
b_baalbak.etymology_analysis: Ancient Semitic/Phoenician name (b'lbk, Arabic Ba'labakk) associated with the god Ba'al and the Beqaa Valley; renamed Heliopolis ('Sun City') after 334 BCE before the indigenous name resurfaced in Arabic.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Heljôpel (Heljôpel; or calqued Ritterburch for Hisn al-Akrad (in-game: Baalbek))
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Anachronistic foundation evaluated in 1122 Imperial Chancellery audit.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Hellenistic renaming following Alexander the Great's conquest (334 BCE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Greco-Roman official name alongside the indigenous Semitic name Baalbak.

b_az-zabadani.first_mention_attestation: Hellenistic-era reference to the local Zabadaioi tribe (conflicting with Alexander Jannaeus, 103-76 BCE)
b_az-zabadani.etymology_analysis: Derived from an Aramaic toponym attested via the Hellenistic ethnonym Zabadaioi in the Anti-Lebanon / Qalamoun region during the 1st century BCE.

b_anjar.first_mention_attestation: Theophanes the Confessor (709-710 CE) and Syriac quarry graffiti (714 CE)
b_anjar.etymology_analysis: Umayyad palace-city founded in 709-710 CE by al-Walid I / al-Abbas on virgin soil; Anjar derives from Arabic Ayn al-Jarr ('spring of running water').

older_name_by_867.notes: Built on virgin soil in 709-710 CE.

b_damascus.first_mention_attestation: Geographical list of Thutmose III (15th century BCE) as tjmsqw and Amarna letters (14th century BCE) as Dimasqa

morphemes.translation: ancient city name of uncertain pre-Semitic or Semitic origin

b_damascus.etymology_analysis: Attested in 15th-century BCE Egyptian (tjmsqw) and 14th-century BCE Akkadian Amarna (Dimasqa) records, continuing through Aramaic Damasq, Greek Damaskos, Latin Damascus, and Arabic Dimashq.

b_nawa.first_mention_attestation: 3rd-century CE Mosaic of Rehob and Midrash Rabba (Neve / Naveh); Bordeaux Pilgrim (333 CE)
b_nawa.etymology_analysis: Principal town of early Islamic Hauran, continuing the Roman-Byzantine Jewish and Christian center attested as Neve / Naveh from the 3rd century CE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: 3rd-century Mosaic of Rehob and Bordeaux Pilgrim (333 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Roman/Byzantine-era Aramaic/Hebrew/Greek forms of the name.

b_darayya.first_mention_attestation: Diocletianic boundary stones (c. 300 CE) as Daron
b_darayya.etymology_analysis: Ancient settlement 8 km southwest of Damascus, identified with Daron on Diocletianic boundary stones erected around 300 CE and continuing into Arabic as Darayya.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Diocletianic boundary stones (c. 300 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Late Roman Greek form of the toponym.

b_zurra.first_mention_attestation: Medieval Arabic sources (1253 CE mosque inscription under an-Nasir Yusuf; Abulfida's Taqwim al-Buldan) as Zur'a / Zura'
b_zurra.etymology_analysis: Medieval Arabic form (Zur'a / Zura', rendered Zurra) of ancient Zorava (modern Izraa), attested in medieval Arabic geographies and Ottoman tax registers (Madinat Zura', 1596).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Amarna letters (1334 BCE) and Roman inscription under Severus Alexander (222-235 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Canaanite, Roman, and Byzantine name (Zorava) for modern Izraa / medieval Zur'a.

b_busra.first_mention_attestation: 14th-century BCE Egyptian sources and 2nd-century BCE Nabataean records
b_busra.etymology_analysis: Ancient Semitic toponym attested in 14th-century BCE Egyptian records, serving as the northern Nabataean capital and Roman provincial capital Bostra before continuing as Arabic Busra.

current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Anachronistic foundation evaluated in 1122 Imperial Chancellery audit.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Roman provincial capital of Arabia Petraea (106 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Greco-Roman name of the city.

b_sarkhad.first_mention_attestation: Hebrew Bible (Salcah) and 1st-century CE Nabataean inscription (57 CE); 6th-century Madaba Map
b_sarkhad.etymology_analysis: Medieval Arabic variant (Sarkhad / Salkhad) of the ancient Hauran/Bashan city Salcah, attested in the Hebrew Bible, Nabataean inscriptions (57 CE), and the 6th-century Madaba Map.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Hebrew Bible and Nabataean inscription (57 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Biblical and Nabataean form of the name.

b_as-suwaida-hauran.first_mention_attestation: Yaqut al-Hamawi (1220s CE) as Suwayda; compound 'As-Suwaida-Hauran' is a modern disambiguated title form
b_as-suwaida-hauran.etymology_analysis: Disambiguated form of As-Suwayda (in the Hauran region), derived from Nabataean Suada (hellenized as Dionysias Soada in 149 CE) and attested in Arabic geographical literature by Yaqut al-Hamawi in the 1220s.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Nabataean foundation Suada, renamed Dionysias in 149 CE
older_name_by_867.notes: Nabataean and Greco-Roman names for the city.

b_juwair.first_mention_attestation: No documented historical attestation found on or before 867 CE

morphemes.translation: unattested toponym (possibly diminutive of jar 'neighbor' or jawr)

b_juwair.etymology_analysis: Toponym used in game geography for a desert/steppe county northeast of Damascus alongside al-Qastal, without a documented historical attestation on or before 867 CE.

b_al-qastal.first_mention_attestation: Yaqut al-Hamawi (early 13th century CE) as a caravan station between Homs and Damascus
b_al-qastal.etymology_analysis: Arabicized from Latin castellum ('fortress'), referring to a caravan stop in the Qalamoun Mountains between Damascus and Homs; first explicitly documented by Yaqut al-Hamawi in the early 13th century.

b_marj-rahit.first_mention_attestation: Battle of Marj Rahit (18 August 684 CE) during the Second Fitna, recorded in early Islamic chronicles (e.g., al-Tabari).
b_marj-rahit.etymology_analysis: Arabic 'Marj Rahit' ('Meadow of Rahit'), a plain in the Ghouta east of Damascus famous as the site of the 684 CE Umayyad victory.

b_aintab.first_mention_attestation: Captured by the Seljuk commander Afshin Bey in 1067 CE; Crusader chronicles record it as Hantab/Hamtab in 1098 CE.
b_aintab.etymology_analysis: Medieval Arabic 'Aintab ('Aīntāb), possibly from Semitic 'ayn ('spring') + tāb/ṭayyib ('good') or Aramaic 'ayin debo ('spring of the wolf'), or Hittite khantap. Later Ottoman Ayıntap and Republican Gaziantep (1921/1928).

current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Anachronistic foundation evaluated in 1122 Imperial Chancellery audit.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Hellenistic foundation (2nd-1st century BCE) identified as the probable ancient site of Gaziantep.
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Antiochia ad Taurum is thought to have stood at the site of modern Gaziantep, while Doliche (Duluk, 12 km north) was the dominant ancient and early medieval city.

b_tall_bashir.first_mention_attestation: Captured in 1097 CE by Baldwin I during the First Crusade (Latin: Turbessel; Syriac: Tel Bshir; Arabic: Tell Bashir).
b_tall_bashir.etymology_analysis: Arabic/Syriac 'Tall Bashir' ('Mound of Bashir'), adapted by Crusaders as Turbessel and in Armenian as T'lpashar.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Ebla tablets (c. 2300 BCE), identified with Tell Bashir by Alfonso Archi (2011).
older_name_by_867.notes: Site was occupied in the Bronze Age as Hassum/Hassuwan before regaining prominence as a Byzantine-Armenian fortress in the late 11th century.

b_jarabulus.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the 18th century as Djerabis / Djeraboolos / Djerablus.
b_jarabulus.etymology_analysis: 18th-century Arabic toponym Djerabis/Jarabulus, derived from Greco-Roman Europos (at nearby Carchemish) or influenced by Hierapolis (Manbij).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Bronze/Iron Age Carchemish (Karkemish) and Hellenistic/Roman Europos.
older_name_by_867.notes: The ancient archaeological site of Carchemish (Hellenistic/Roman Europos) lies immediately north of modern Jarabulus.

b_duluk-teluch.first_mention_attestation: Modern/scholarly compound of Arabic Duluk (7th c. CE) and medieval Armenian/Crusader Tluk/Tulupa (late 11th c. CE).
b_duluk-teluch.etymology_analysis: Compound of the Arabic form Duluk and the Armenian form Tluk' (Crusader Tulupa), both derived from Ancient Greek Doliche.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Greek Doliche attested in 2nd-century CE literary sources (and 3rd-2nd c. BCE amphorae); Arabic Duluk after the 7th-century Muslim conquest by Iyad ibn Ghanm.
older_name_by_867.notes: Greek Doliche and early Islamic Duluk are both attested well before 867 CE; the hyphenated compound Duluk-Teluch incorporates the post-867 Armenian/Crusader form.

b_edessa.first_mention_attestation: Founded c. 303 BCE by Seleucus I Nicator and named Edessa after the ancient Macedonian capital.
b_edessa.etymology_analysis: Ancient Greek Edessa, transferred by Seleucus I Nicator from Edessa in Macedonia to the Syriac settlement of Urhay/Orhay.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Pre-Seleucid Syriac name Urhay / Orhay (later Arabic ar-Ruha, modern Turkish Urfa/Şanlıurfa).
older_name_by_867.notes: Syriac Urhay/Orhay was the indigenous name prior to Seleucus I's refoundation as Edessa.

b_al-bira.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Bithra (Greek Βίθρα for Birtha) in Zosimus's account of Emperor Julian's 363 CE campaign; Syriac Birtha at Chalcedon (451 CE) and Arabic al-Bira in medieval sources.
b_al-bira.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Bira, directly borrowed from Aramaic/Syriac Birtha ('fortress'); later Turkish Birecik with diminutive suffix -cik.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Macedonopolis attested at the First Council of Nicaea (325 CE); Birtha/Bithra in Zosimus (363 CE) and Syriac texts (451 CE).
older_name_by_867.notes: Aramaic/Syriac Birtha and Greek Macedonopolis were the pre-Islamic names of the Euphrates crossing.

b_marash.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Marqas in Neo-Assyrian records upon the annexation of Gurgum in 711 BCE; Arabic Mar'ash from the 7th century CE.
b_marash.etymology_analysis: Arabic Mar'ash (Turkish Maraş, Armenian Marash), continuing Neo-Assyrian Marqas (capital of Gurgum); renamed Kahramanmaraş in 1973.

current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Anachronistic foundation evaluated in 1122 Imperial Chancellery audit.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Iron Age Syro-Hittite capital of Gurgum (11th c. BCE) / Neo-Assyrian Marqas (711 BCE); Roman Germanicia Caesarea (1st c. CE, attested at Nicaea 325 CE).
older_name_by_867.notes: Called Germanicia (Germanikeia) during the Roman and Byzantine eras before the revival of the Semitic name Mar'ash/Marash.

b_qalat_ar-rum.first_mention_attestation: Armenian Hromgla attested from the late 11th century (c. 1071-1087 under Philaretos Brachamios); Arabic Qal'at ar-Rum in 12th-13th century sources (1292 Mamluk siege).
b_qalat_ar-rum.etymology_analysis: Arabic Qal'at ar-Rum ('Citadel of the Romans'), calqued from/parallel to Armenian Hromgla and Turkish Rumkale.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Qal'at ar-Rum / Hromgla (Arabic/Armenian 'Citadel of the Romans' on the Euphrates) (in-game: Rômerburch)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Descriptive Near Eastern fortress toponym calqued to Tarraconian Rômerburch.

older_name_by_867.notes: Foundations date back to Byzantine rule at the earliest, with no verified pre-867 distinct settlement name.

b_kaisum.first_mention_attestation: Fortified as Kaysum/Kaysun around 812 CE by Nasr ibn Shabath al-Uqayli and besieged by the Abbasids in October 823 CE; Syriac Orthodox bishopric in the early 9th century.
b_kaisum.etymology_analysis: Early medieval Arabic Kaysum/Kaysun (Armenian K'esun), evolving from the Roman road station name Kessos.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Roman road station Kessos on the route from Germanicia to Samosata.
older_name_by_867.notes: Known as Kessos in Roman antiquity before becoming the early medieval frontier town of Kaysum.

b_samosata.first_mention_attestation: Founded before 245 BCE by the Orontid king Sames I of Sophene.
b_samosata.eponym_details: Named after Sames I, Orontid king of Sophene (c. 260-245 BCE), from Middle/Old Persian *Sāmašād / *Sāmašiyāti- ('joy of Sames').
b_samosata.etymology_analysis: Hellenized Greek Samosata from Iranian *Sāmašiyāti- ('Joy of Sames'), an Orontid royal foundation on the upper Euphrates.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Neo-Hittite / Luwian city and kingdom of Kummuh prior to the Hellenistic foundation of Samosata.
older_name_by_867.notes: Built on the earlier Neo-Hittite site of Kummuh.

b_bahasna.first_mention_attestation: Captured by the Umayyad army in 670 CE under the historical name Bahasna.
b_bahasna.etymology_analysis: Medieval Arabic/Syriac toponym Bahasna, later shortened in Turkish/Kurdish to Besni/Bêsnî.

b_hama.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Hamath (Assyrian: Amat/Hamata) in Shalmaneser III's inscriptions of 853 BCE and in the Hebrew Bible; restored as Hama after the 638 CE Muslim conquest.
b_hama.etymology_analysis: Semitic toponym Hamath ('fortress'), attested since the Iron Age, renamed Epiphania in the Hellenistic period, and restored as Arabic Hama after 638 CE.

current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Anachronistic foundation evaluated in 1122 Imperial Chancellery audit.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Renamed Epiphania in the 2nd century BCE under Antiochus IV Epiphanes (used in Greco-Roman and ecclesiastical records); Iron Age Hamath (853 BCE).
older_name_by_867.notes: Known in Greco-Roman antiquity and Byzantine ecclesiastical lists as Epiphania.

b_salamiya.first_mention_attestation: Conquered by Muslim Arabs in 636 CE and settled by the Abbasid dynasty after 750 CE as Salamiya (Salamiyya), continuing Byzantine Salaminias/Salamias.
b_salamiya.etymology_analysis: Arabic Salamiyya, adapted from the Byzantine town name Salaminias / Salamias.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Bishop Julian of Salamias attended the consecration of Patriarch Severus of Antioch in 512 CE.
older_name_by_867.notes: Flourished as Byzantine Salaminias/Salamias prior to the 636 CE Muslim conquest.

b_kafartab.first_mention_attestation: Mentioned during the Second Fitna (680 CE) among Syrian towns mourning Husayn ibn Ali, and described by al-Ya'qubi in the late 9th century.
b_kafartab.etymology_analysis: Aramaic-Arabic compound Kafr Tab ('Good Village'), Latinized by the Crusaders as Capharda.

b_hims.first_mention_attestation: Arabic Hims (from pre-Islamic Emesa, attested 1st century BCE) established as capital of Jund Hims following the 7th-century Muslim conquest (c. 637 CE).
b_hims.etymology_analysis: Arabic Hims (modern Homs), derived from the classical name Emesa (1st century BCE).

current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Anachronistic foundation evaluated in 1122 Imperial Chancellery audit.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Entered historical record in the 1st century BCE as Emesa, capital of the Emesene dynasty.
older_name_by_867.notes: Known in Greco-Roman and Byzantine times as Emesa prior to the 7th-century Muslim conquest.

b_rafaniya-krak.first_mention_attestation: Composite of ancient Raphanea (70 CE) and Krak des Chevaliers, granted to the Knights Hospitaller in 1142 CE.
b_rafaniya-krak.etymology_analysis: Modern/game composite combining the nearby Roman-Byzantine city of Raphanea (al-Rafaniyya) with the 12th-century Crusader fortress Krak des Chevaliers.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Ancient Roman and Byzantine civitas Raphanea (in-game: Rafaniya-Krak)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: 1142 Hospitaller fortress Krak des Chevaliers fails Burden of Proof on Antiquity; restored to ancient Raphanea.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Flavius Josephus mentions Raphanea in connection with Titus's march in 70 CE; later garrison of Legio III Gallica.
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Raphanea (al-Rafaniyya) is attested from the 1st century CE, whereas Krak des Chevaliers dates to 1031/1142 CE.

b_jusiya.first_mention_attestation: Listed by Arab geographer al-Muqaddasi in 985 CE among the principal towns of Jund Qinnasrin.
b_jusiya.etymology_analysis: Medieval Arabic toponym Jusiya (modern Jusiyah / al-Jousieh), located south of Homs near al-Qusayr.

b_shayzar.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Senzar / Sezar in the Amarna letters (14th century BCE), continuing as Roman/Byzantine Sezer and Arabic Shayzar.
b_shayzar.etymology_analysis: Arabic Shayzar preserves the Bronze Age Semitic name Senzar/Sezar, which briefly yielded to Hellenistic Larissa before reverting under Rome and Islam.

current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Resolved via verified historical center Larîsse-in-Sîrjen documented in tarraconian_titles_1059.md.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Amarna letters (14th century BCE) as Senzar/Sezar; renamed Larissa in the Seleucid period.
older_name_by_867.notes: Renamed Larissa in Syria under the Seleucids before reverting to its indigenous name (Sezer/Shayzar).

b_masyaf.first_mention_attestation: Masyaf and its fortress were first mentioned by Crusader chroniclers in 1099 CE.
b_masyaf.etymology_analysis: Arabic Masyaf (pronounced Maṣyaf/Maṣyat/Maṣyad), evolved from Assyrian Mansuate ('raised platform'), referring to the promontory of the fortress.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: 8th-century BCE Aramean/Assyrian city of Mansuate; Roman/Byzantine Marsyas.
older_name_by_867.notes: Site corresponds to ancient Mansuate and Greco-Roman Marsyas prior to the medieval attestation of Masyaf in 1099 CE.

b_beirut.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Biruta in three Akkadian cuneiform tablets of the Amarna letters (14th century BCE).
b_beirut.etymology_analysis: Arabic Bayrut (English Beirut) from Phoenician bēʾrūt ('wells'), Hellenized as Berytos and Latinized as Berytus.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Amarna letters (Biruta, 14th century BCE) and Greco-Roman Berytos/Berytus.
older_name_by_867.notes: Bronze Age Biruta and Greco-Roman Berytus represent earlier attested forms of the same name.

b_saida.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Egyptian Papyrus Anastasi I (13th century BCE) as ḏjdwnꜣ and in Phoenician as Ṣīdūn (Biblical Hebrew Ṣīḏōn); Arabic Ṣaydā.
b_saida.etymology_analysis: Arabic Saida (Ṣaydā), continuing Classical Arabic Ṣaydūn and Phoenician Ṣīdūn ('fishery'), known in English via Greek/Latin as Sidon.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Phoenician Sidon (Papyrus Anastasi I, 13th century BCE; Biblical Hebrew Ṣīḏōn).
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Phoenician and Greco-Roman Sidon is the classical form of Arabic Saida.

b_syrtripolis.first_mention_attestation: Named Tripolis ('three cities') by Greek settlers in the Classical/Hellenistic period (attested by the 4th century BCE); Arabic Tarabulus.
b_syrtripolis.etymology_analysis: Greek Tripolis ('three cities', referring to the confederation of Sidon, Tyre, and Aradus), borrowed into Arabic as Tarabulus.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Phoenician Athar, dating back at least to the 14th century BCE.
older_name_by_867.notes: Known as Athar by the Phoenicians prior to the Greek name Tripolis.

b_antartus.first_mention_attestation: Crusader Latinization Antartus (alongside Tortosa) attested from the First Crusade (1099 CE), derived from Greek Antarados and Arabic Antartus/Tartus.
b_antartus.etymology_analysis: Crusader form Antartus (also Tortosa), adapted from Arabic Anṭarṭūs/Ṭarṭūs, itself from Ancient Greek Antarados ('the town facing Aradus').

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Antaradus attested in Late Roman/Byzantine ecclesiastical records (4th century CE under Constantine; Councils of Ephesus 431 and Chalcedon 451).
older_name_by_867.notes: Phoenician and Greco-Roman Antaradus (facing the island of Aradus) is the ancient name of Tartus.

b_tadmur.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Ta-ad-mi-ir in 18th-century BCE cuneiform tablets from Mari, and Ta-ad-mar in 11th-century BCE Assyrian inscriptions.
b_tadmur.etymology_analysis: Arabic Tadmur preserves the Bronze Age Semitic name Ta-ad-mi-ir/Tadmar, which was adapted in Greco-Roman antiquity as Palmyra.

current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Anachronistic foundation evaluated in 1122 Imperial Chancellery audit.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Greek/Latin Palmyra first recorded by Pliny the Elder in the 1st century CE.
older_name_by_867.notes: Known in Greco-Roman antiquity as Palmyra, while the indigenous Semitic name Tadmur persisted and remained standard in Arabic.

b_arak.first_mention_attestation: Roman milestones from 75 CE and a 209 CE altar attest the settlement as Aracha; conquered by Khalid ibn al-Walid in 634 CE as Arak.
b_arak.etymology_analysis: Arabic Arak, continuing Roman-era Aracha on the desert road between Palmyra and Sura.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Roman milestone of 75 CE under governor Marcus Ulpius Traianus and 209 CE altar to Yarhibol.
older_name_by_867.notes: Aracha is the Roman Latinized form of the same Semitic settlement name.

b_al-qaryatan.first_mention_attestation: Conquered by Khalid ibn al-Walid in the summer of 634 CE under the Arabic name al-Qaryatayn.
b_al-qaryatan.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Qaryatayn ('the two villages'), an oasis town in the Syrian Desert between Homs and Palmyra.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Palmyrene/Roman inscriptions in the town dedicated to the 'Great God of Nazala'.
older_name_by_867.notes: Known in the Roman/Palmyrene period as Nazala.

b_judr.first_mention_attestation: No verified historical attestation found for 'Judr' in the Qaryatayn/Palmyra region in Wikipedia or standard historical gazetteers.
b_judr.etymology_analysis: Unverified medieval/game barony name in the Qaryatayn district; no pre-867 or medieval attestation located.

b_as-sukhna.first_mention_attestation: Submitted peacefully to Khalid ibn al-Walid's Rashidun army in 634 CE following the capture of Arak.

morphemes.translation: warm, hot (feminine, referring to the warm sulphur springs)

b_as-sukhna.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Sukhnah ('the Warm [Springs]'), named after the nearby thermal sulphur springs in the Syrian Desert oasis.

b_dair_ar-ruman.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Dayr al-Rumman ('Monastery of the Pomegranates') in Yaqut al-Hamawi's Mu'jam al-Buldan (1225 CE).
b_dair_ar-ruman.etymology_analysis: Arabic Dayr al-Rumman ('Monastery of the Pomegranates'), a medieval name for the Euphrates settlement later known as Deir ez-Zor.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Roman Azura / Auzara and early Islamic al-Firad at the site of Deir ez-Zor.
older_name_by_867.notes: Occupied in Roman times as Azura and in early Islamic times as al-Firad before being recorded as Dayr al-Rumman by Yaqut al-Hamawi.

b_urd.first_mention_attestation: Attested as 'Urd in Yaqut al-Hamawi's Mu'jam al-Buldan (1225 CE) as a district/locality in the Syrian Desert near al-Sukhnah and al-Taybah.
b_urd.etymology_analysis: Medieval Arabic toponym 'Urd, associated with the oasis of al-Taybah northeast of al-Sukhnah in the Syrian Desert.
